To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

extracellular flux analyses (XF) is a powerful tool to study mitochondrial dysfunction and that caution must be used to assure that the appropriate developmental stage of cardiomyocyte is being studied.
the bioenergetics of isolated neonatal and adult rat cardiomyocytes differ significantly and these differences must be considered when using extracellular flux analyses to study cardiac disease.
the bioenergetic profiles of cardiomyocytes change with age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel method to investigate mitochondrial function and dysfunction in the context of heart disease.
the study of mitochondrial bioenergetics and its role in the development of heart disease.
the role of the mitochondria, the energy-producing powerhouses of the cell, in the pathogenesis of heart disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this study provides a foundation for the use of extracellular flux analysis (Seahorse) as a tool to study mitochondrial dysfunction and bioenergetics of cardiomyocytes in the context of heart disease.

the use of isolated cardiomyocytes from newborn rats should be reserved to investigate neonatal disease and the use of older cardiomyocytes (≥10 weeks old) should be used for adult disease pathogenesis.
there are age-related changes in mitochondrial and glycolytic function in rat CMs, which should be considered when designing studies to investigate cardiac disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of newborn CMs to investigate adult cardiac disease is not appropriate and that the use of adult CMs to study neonatal cardiac disease is not optimal.
there is a developmental shift from glycolysis to mitochondrial respiration that occurs in rat cardiomyocytes (rat hearts).
we have established the bioenergetics differences in isolated cardiomyocytes at various stages of development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bioenergetics profile of cardiomyocytes (heart cells) changes dramatically as they mature from newborn to adult.
the bioenergetic profiles of isolated rat CMs change dramatically as the cells mature.
caution should be used when comparing bioenergetic profiles of cardiomyocytes at different developmental time points.
